annotations.annotation_text: Page 34 opens Book 1, Chapter 2 ("The Encounter in Phoenix Park") during the Age of Gods phase. This passage continues HCE's mysterious sin in Phoenix Park, the spread of gossip through Dublin, and the Cad with the pipe, featuring HCE, the Cad, Hosty. The nocturnal dream-narrative layers Dublin topography, world mythology, and linguistic alchemy into polysemic prose.

annotations.annotation_text: The Cad's innocent query (034.12): walking in Phoenix Park around high noon, a casual loafer ('cad') simply asks HCE for the time of day. HCE's guilty conscience transforms this innocuous question into an extortion attempt.
sources: Campbell, Joseph and Robinson, Henry Morton. A Skeleton Key. https://archive.org/details/skeletonkeytofin00camp

annotations.annotation_text: HCE manifestation "Earwicker" on page 34 within "The Encounter in Phoenix Park": here the universal father-figure Humphrey Chimpden Earwicker appears in the context of HCE's mysterious sin in Phoenix Park, the spread of gossip through Dublin, and the Cad with the pipe. During this Age of Gods phase, HCE embodies the patriarch whose guilt, grandeur, and fall drive the cyclical dream forward.
sources: Glasheen, Adaline. Third Census of Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/thirdcensusoffin0000glas

annotations.annotation_text: Mid-page polysemic node on page 34 ("The Encounter in Phoenix Park"): Joyce weaves multilingual puns across 60+ languages — etymological roots from the Contemporary Literature Press lexicons (Romanian, Scandinavian, Slavic, Classical) intersect with local Dublin speech rhythms. The Age of Gods dream-logic transforms ordinary syntax into a palimpsest of global literary and mythic references.
sources: Tindall, William York. A Reader's Guide to Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/readersguidetofi00tind
Contemporary Literature Press: Multilingual Lexicons for FW. https://editura.mttlc.ro
Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: Double pun "luciferant" (034.30): the Cad strikes a friction match ('lucifer') to light his pipe, while functioning symbolically as Lucifer, the accuser and light-bringer who exposes the patriarch's secret guilt.

Shakespearean echo "cad with a pipe" (034.32): alludes to Hamlet (I.ii.200) where the ghost of King Hamlet is described as armed 'from top to toe' or 'cap-a-pe' (Old French de cap à pié). The Cad becomes the phantom witness demanding justice.
sources: Atherton, James S. The Books at the Wake. https://archive.org/details/booksatwake0000athe

annotations.annotation_text: Unsolicited denial (034.34): trembling in defensive paranoia, HCE raises his right hand and vehemently denies having committed any indecent act with the two maidens or the three soldiers, convicting himself through unprompted protestation.
sources: Gordon, John. Finnegans Wake: A Plot Summary. https://johngordonfinnegan.weebly.com
